blocks.b:
Rickenbacker는 자사 연혁에서 the Electro String Instrument Corporation을 완전 전기식 악기와 앰프를 만들기 위해서만 세워진 최초의 회사로 소개한다. 첫 제품의 연도는 1931년.

악기는 랩스틸이었다. 별명은 Frying Pan이었다.

media.note: 정면 누끼. 후보: Wikimedia 'Flying Pan prototype (1931)' CC BY-SA 2.0 / 대안: 특허 Fig.1 도면(PD)

blocks.b:
George Beauchamp는 1920년대 로스앤젤레스에서 스틸 기타를 치던 연주자였다. 그는 더 큰 소리가 나는 기타를 원했다.

그는 National에서 Dopyera 형제와 함께 금속 바디 리조네이터 기타를 만들었다. 동업은 틀어졌다. John Dopyera가 National 주식은 그대로 쥔 채 회사를 나가 Dobro를 차렸고, Beauchamp도 결국 밀려났다.

media.note: National 트라이콘 리조네이터 기타 / 선택: 1930년대 하와이안 밴드 연주 아카이브 영상

blocks.b:
Beauchamp은 1925년 무렵부터 실험을 거듭했다. 1930년에는 말굽자석 두 개로 만든 픽업에 도달한다. 자석 사이를 지나는 줄 아래로, 폴피스 여섯 개를 꽂은 코일이 놓이는 구조였다.

Rickenbacker의 연혁은 그 과정을 “여러 달에 걸친 시행착오”라고 적는다.

media.note: 혼스슈 픽업 클로즈업 + 특허 Fig.2 단면도. 스크롤로 자석·코일·줄 레이어를 하나씩 켜는 연출
media.caption: The horseshoe pickup. The strings pass between the magnet arms, over a coil with six pole pieces.

blocks.b:
픽업이 제대로 울리자 Beauchamp은 Harry Watson을 찾아갔다. National의 공장장을 지낸 솜씨 좋은 장인이다.

Watson은 수공구만으로 몇 시간 만에 넥과 바디를 깎아냈다. 회사는 이것을 최초의 완전 전기식 기타라고 부르고, 별명이 붙은 이유에 대해서는 “보면 안다”고만 적어두었다.

양산하려면 설비가 필요했다. Beauchamp이 끌어들인 사람이 Adolph Rickenbacker다. 스위스 태생의 생산 기술자로, 서부 해안에서 손꼽히는 대형 딥드로잉 프레스를 가지고 있었다. 이미 National에 금속 바디를 납품하던 사람이었다.

회사는 1931년 로스앤젤레스에서 Ro-Pat-In Corporation이라는 이름으로 출발해 곧 Electro String으로 바꿨다. Adolph가 사장, Beauchamp이 재무 담당 임원을 맡았다. 생산은 사우스 웨스턴 애비뉴 6071번지의 작은 임대 공장에서 시작됐다. Rickenbacker의 금형 공장 바로 옆이었다.

악기에 Rickenbacker라는 이름이 붙은 이유는 둘이다. Adolph가 1차 대전 격추왕 Eddie Rickenbacker의 친척이었고, Beauchamp보다 부르기 쉬웠다.

media.note: 초기 Electro String 로고 또는 1930년대 카탈로그 표지 / 공장 위치 그래픽(6071 S. Western Ave, LA)
media.caption: Rickenbacker Electro nameplate, Los Angeles.

blocks.b:
Beauchamp은 1932년 6월 8일에 출원했다. 심사는 멈춰 섰다. Rickenbacker의 설명에 따르면 특허청은 Frying Pan이 전기 장치인지 악기인지 판단하지 못했고, 둘 다를 담는 분류가 없었다.

그는 1934년 6월 2일 계속출원으로 다시 냈다. 미국 특허 2,089,171호는 1937년 8월 10일에 등록된다. 첫 출원으로부터 5년이 지난 뒤였다.

명세서는 발명의 목적 하나를 이렇게 적는다. “원하는 음질을 내거나 전달하는 데 사운드보드나 공명통 따위에 의존하지 아니하며, 그리하여 악기의 몸통을 단순하고 저렴한 구조로 할 수 있도록 하는 것.”

줄에 대해서는 이렇게 쓴다. “양 끝이 강성의 금속 몸통에 견고하고 유격 없이 결합되어, 목재 몸통부가 진동을 흡수하여 감쇠시키는 일 없이 그 대부분이 오래 진동할 수 있도록 한다.”

media.note: US2089171 1페이지 전문(PD, 고해상도 확보). 스크롤에 따라 도면 선이 그려지는 연출
media.caption: U.S. Patent 2,089,171, filed 1932, granted 1937.

blocks.b:
양산형 Frying Pan은 Watson이 깎은 나무가 아니라 알루미늄 주물이었다. 특허는 몸통을 “알루미늄 따위 금속의 단순한 일체 주조물”이라 적는다.

6현과 7현, 스케일은 22.5인치와 25인치로 나왔다. Rickenbacker의 연혁은 이 모델이 1950년대까지 카탈로그에 남아 있었다고 쓴다.

알루미늄은 무대 조명 아래서 늘어난다. 넥이 데워지면 음이 올라갔다.

media.note: 알루미늄 바디·넥 디테일, 내부 신문지 샷 + 스펙 박스
media.caption: Stripped for service. Body and neck are a single aluminium casting.

blocks.b:
폴피스 여섯 개가 자석의 두 팔 사이에서 줄마다 하나씩 자리를 잡는다. 악기에 달린 노브는 볼륨 하나뿐이다.

브리지는 주물 상판에 나사로 고정한 판이다. 그 아래에는 울릴 것이 없다.

media.caption: Bridge plate, pickup, volume control and the output jack in the rim.

blocks.b: 원본을 직접 연주하며 설명하는 영상.

1940년, 15년을 쉬지 않고 달린 Beauchamp은 악기 사업에 지쳐 있었다. 건강도 나빠지고 있었다. 그는 Electro String 지분을 회사 경리였던 Harold Kinney에게 넘겼다. 자기가 특허를 낸 낚시용 루어에 돈을 대기 위해서였다.

그는 바다낚시를 하던 중 심장마비로 숨졌다. Rickenbacker의 기록은 장례 행렬이 2마일, 3킬로미터 넘게 이어졌다고 적는다.

Adolph Rickenbacker는 1953년까지 악기를 만들었다. 그해 그와 다른 주주들은 지분을 Francis C. Hall에게 넘긴다. the Radio and Television Equipment Company를 운영하며 1946년부터 Leo Fender의 독점 유통을 맡아온 사람이었다.

Rickenbacker는 이 매각을 지금 회사의 출발점으로 본다. Electro String은 법인으로는 아직 남아 있다. 이름만 훗날의 합병을 거쳐 Rickenbacker International Corporation으로 바뀌었다.
Gibson은 자사 연혁에서 과제를 이렇게 정리한다. 첫 전기 기타에 착수할 무렵 회사에는 지켜야 할 40년의 전통이 있었고, 따라서 “Gibson의 첫 일렉트릭은 세상이 본 적 없는 최고의 전기 기타여야만 했다.”

media.note: 정면 누끼. 후보: 'Gibson Electro Spanish-150, Prototype Batch (1936), Museum of Making Music' CC BY-SA 2.0, 2448px

blocks.b:
1935년 봄, Gibson은 음악가 Alvino Rey를 끌어들여 시카고 Lyon & Healy의 엔지니어들과 함께 시제품 픽업을 개발하게 했다. 그해 후반 연구는 사내로 옮겨졌고, 직원 Walter Fuller가 최종 설계를 내놓는다.

그렇게 나온 육각형 픽업은 1935년 말 랩스틸 모델에 먼저 올라갔다.

media.note: 1935~36년 깁슨 칼라마주 공장 사진 또는 EH-150 랩스틸 이미지

blocks.b: 이 픽업을 f홀 아치탑에 얹은 것이 ES-150이다. ES는 일렉트릭 스패니시의 약자다. 첫 대가 미시간주 칼라마주 공장에서 출하된 날은 1936년 5월 20일이었다.

Guy Hart는 1936년 2월 8일에 특허를 출원해 둔 상태였다. 명세서가 밝힌 목적은 이렇다.

“첫째, 실질적으로 공명하지 아니하는 몸통 부재와, 그 위에서 만들어진 음악을 원하는 정도까지 증폭하는 수단을 갖춘 전기 증폭식 현악기를 제공하는 것. 둘째, 진동하는 줄이 만들어내는 공극의 변화만으로 증폭이 이루어지는 악기를 제공하는 것. 셋째, 외관이 아름다운 악기를 제공하는 것.”

방법도 적혀 있다. “본인은 악기의 몸통을, 공명성이 실질적으로 결여된 비교적 두꺼운 경질 목재 또는 금속 벽으로 설계하였다.”

Gibson은 이 문서를 내놓고, 속이 빈 아치탑을 출하했다.

media.note: US2087106 Fig.1 (퍼블릭 도메인). 기타와 앰프가 케이블로 이어진 도면이라 '앰프가 있어야 완성되는 악기'라는 개념을 그대로 보여줌. 스크롤에 따라 선이 그려지는 연출

blocks.b:
16.25인치 아치탑. 스프루스 상판을 깎아 올리고 측후판은 메이플, 넥은 마호가니, 지판은 로즈우드, 트러스로드는 조절식이었다.

자석과 코일은 몸통 안에 들어간다. 상판 위로 드러나는 것은 블레이드 하나뿐이다. 줄마다 폴피스를 두는 대신 여섯 줄 아래를 하나의 막대가 가로지르고, 그 자리는 지판이 끝나는 지점이다.

media.note: 픽업 클로즈업(지판 끝에 붙은 위치가 보이게) + 바디 측면. 1937 카탈로그 35쪽 스캔을 보조로

blocks.b:
Charlie Christian은 1939년부터 1942년까지 Benny Goodman과 연주했다. Gibson의 연혁은 그가 “전기 기타를 고유한 목소리를 가진 악기로 자리잡게 했다”고 쓴다.

60년이 지난 지금도 ES-150은 Charlie Christian 모델로 불리며, 일부 재즈 연주자는 이 픽업을 역사상 최고의 재즈 픽업으로 꼽는다고 회사는 덧붙인다.

Christian은 1942년 결핵으로 세상을 떠났다. 스물다섯이었다.

media.note: 찰리 크리스천 사진 + 1939~41년 베니 굿맨 섹스텟 녹음 클립. 사진 저작권 확인 필요

blocks.b:
모델은 그대로 머물지 않았다. 1940년 들어 판매가 꺾이자 손질이 들어갔고, 당시 신소재였던 알니코 자석을 쓴 픽업이 올라갔다. 1948년에는 ES-150에 처음으로 픽업 두 개를 단 사양이 나온다.

Gibson은 결과를 양날의 칼로 설명한다. ES-150의 성공은 회사를 전기 기타 분야의 선두로 올려놓았고, 동시에 그 성과를 넘어서야 하는 숙제를 남겼다. 그리고 생산은 2차 대전으로 끊긴다.

Gibson 카탈로그의 광고 문구는 “완벽한 전기 스패니시 기타”였다.

media.note: ES-150_01 — 앰프와 함께 선 전신 사진. changes·impact·coda 병합

blocks.b:
Gibson은 ES-175를 스스로 ‘혁신의 황금기’라 부르는 시기에 놓는다. 2차 대전이 끝난 뒤, 사장 Ted McCarty가 공격적으로 회사를 끌던 시절이다.

1949년 Gibson은 두 가지를 동시에 내놓았다. 픽업을 셋 단 최초의 기타 ES-5, 그리고 “컷어웨이를 날카롭게 깎아낸 최초의 기타” ES-175다.

media.note: 정면 누끼. 후보: Wikimedia 'Gibson 1959 VOS ES-175' CC BY 2.0 1733px (재현품) 또는 'Herb Ellis 1953 Gibson ES-175' CC BY-SA 4.0 2540px

blocks.b:
전쟁 전의 최상급 아치탑은 덩치가 컸다. Stromberg 마스터 400은 로어 바웃이 19인치, Epiphone 엠퍼러가 18.5인치, Gibson 자신의 슈퍼 400이 18인치였다.

손으로 깎아 만들었으니 비쌌고, 픽업을 달고 앰프를 올리면 울어댔다.

media.note: Gibson Super 400이나 Stromberg Master 400 같은 대형 아치탑 사진. ES-175와 크기를 나란히 비교하는 그래픽으로 만들면 더 좋음

blocks.b:
ES-175는 Gibson이 깎은 통판 대신 합판 메이플 상판으로 만든 첫 아치탑이다. 훗날 Gibson 자신의 설명도 바디와 상판, 측후판을 모두 합판 메이플로 적고 있다.

합판은 싸게 만드는 방법이다. 동시에 깎은 상판보다 단단하고 덜 살아 있다. 음량을 올려도 피드백이 잘 걸리지 않는 이유가 거기 있다.

media.note: f홀 안쪽으로 합판 단면과 평행 브레이스가 보이는 사진. 또는 카브드 탑 vs 합판 탑 단면 비교 다이어그램

blocks.b:
Gibson의 아치탑은 둥근 베네치안 컷어웨이를 써왔다. ES-175는 뾰족했다.

유래는 정리되지 않았다. 이 모델에 관한 책을 쓴 Adrian Ingram은, 젊은 Kenny Burrell이 Charlie Christian 픽업을 단 블론드 L-5를 들고 와 뿔을 더 깊이 파달라고 했다는 이야기를 전한다. 그런 기타를 든 Burrell의 사진은 남아 있다. 그 기타와 이 설계를 잇는 기록은 없다.

media.note: 뾰족한 플로렌틴 컷어웨이 클로즈업. 둥근 베네치안 컷어웨이와 나란히 비교하면 차이가 바로 보임

blocks.b:
로어 바웃 16.25인치, 두께 3.375인치. 마호가니 넥을 14프렛에서 접합하고, 프렛은 19개, 인레이는 더블 패럴렐로그램, 헤드스톡에는 크라운을 넣었다.

넥 포지션에 도그이어 P-90 하나. Gibson이 1946년에 내놓은 픽업이다. 선버스트가 기본, 내추럴은 웃돈을 받았다.

media.note: P-90 도그이어 픽업 클로즈업 + 더블 패럴렐로그램 인레이. 상판에 직접 박힌 토글 스위치도 보이게

blocks.b:
1950년대 초에 픽업 두 개짜리 ES-175D가 따라 나왔다. 1957년에는 P-90 자리를 Gibson의 새 험버커가 대신한다. 픽업 하나짜리 모델은 1971년까지 이어졌다.

부속은 Gibson의 통상 순서를 밟았다. 1953년에 배럴 노브에서 스피드 노브로, 1955년 보닛, 1960년 리플렉터, 1966년 위치햇. 연식을 짚을 때 대개 이 노브를 본다.

media.note: P-90 → PAF 험버커 교체를 보여주는 두 장 비교. 연도별 노브 변화(배럴 → 스피드 → 보닛 → 리플렉터 → 위치햇) 타임라인 그래픽도 가능

blocks.b:
Herb Ellis, Joe Pass, Jim Hall, Wes Montgomery, Pat Metheny가 모두 이 모델을 썼다. 상당수는 픽업 두 개짜리를 사놓고 넥 픽업만 썼다.

재즈에만 머물지도 않았다. Steve Howe가 Yes에서 썼고, Scotty Moore가 초기 Elvis 녹음에서 친 금색 ES-295는 부속만 다를 뿐 같은 바디다.

media.note: 허브 엘리스 또는 조 패스 연주 사진 + 1950~70년대 재즈 기타 녹음 클립. 라이선스 확인 필요

blocks.b: Pat Metheny는 자기 ES-175에서 브리지 픽업과 관련 컨트롤을 들어내고 구멍을 테이프로 막았다. 나머지 부분은 수십 년치 수리 기록이다. 트레블 쪽 f홀 안에 마이크를 넣었고, 튜너를 갈았고, 어느 시점엔가 헤드스톡에 바인딩이 둘러졌으며, 떨어져 나간 스트랩 버튼 자리에는 칫솔이 꽂혀 있다.

credit.ko: 3D 모델: “Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic” — sgab_viz (Sketchfab), CC BY-NC 4.0
credit.ja: 3Dモデル: “Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic” — sgab_viz (Sketchfab), CC BY-NC 4.0

blocks.b:
Fender는 왜 이 기타를 만들었는지 이렇게 설명한다. 1950년 이전까지 회사는 랩스틸과 앰프에 집중했고, 그 분야에서 잘하고 있었다. 그런데 Django Reinhardt, Charlie Christian, T-Bone Walker, Muddy Waters, Big Bill Broonzy 같은 연주자들이 점점 전기 기타를 끌어들이기 시작했다. “우리도 ‘스패니시 스타일’ 모델을 하나 내놓고 싶어지는 게 당연했다.”

“그 필요에서 Broadcaster가 태어났다. 현대 음악가의 요구에 맞춰 만들어진 최초의 솔리드바디 전기 기타 가운데 하나다.”

Broadcaster는 이 기타의 첫 이름이다. 1951년 가을에는 Telecaster가 된다.

media.note: 3D 모델(Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic) — 들머리·전체 모습

blocks.b:
먼저 나온 것은 픽업 하나짜리 Esquire, 1950년이다. Fender는 이것을 파인 바디에 볼트온 메이플 넥, 그리고 랩스틸에서 가져다 쓴 픽업 하나를 브리지에 얹은 악기로 설명한다.

같은 해에 픽업 둘을 단 Broadcaster가 뒤따랐다. 훗날의 Telecaster다.

설계에 대한 Fender 자신의 묘사는 이렇다. “싱글 컷어웨이에 직관적인 2픽업 구성, 노브 둘과 3단 스위치라는 간결한 컨트롤, 여기에 검은 픽가드로 대비를 준 선명한 블론드 피니시를 더한, 효율적인 솔리드바디 일꾼.”

넥은 메이플 한 덩어리에 프렛을 직접 박아 넣었고, 나사 네 개로 볼트온한다. 줄은 바디를 관통해 뒤쪽에서 고정된다. 브리지에는 여섯 줄을 받치는 황동 새들 세 개가 올라간다.

media.note: 브리지 플레이트 3새들 클로즈업 + 넥 조인트 나사 4개 + 몸통 뒷면 줄 구멍. 분해 도식으로 '부품의 집합'임을 보여주기

blocks.b:
Leo Fender는 1950년 1월 13일, 브리지와 픽업을 하나의 조립체로 묶어 출원했다. 기타에 이름이 붙기도 전이다. 명세서가 적은 목적은 제조 지침서처럼 읽힌다.

“첫째, 전기 증폭식 기타 및 유사 악기에 특히 적합하며, 줄마다 개별 조정이 가능한 신규의 분할식 브리지를 포함하는 장치를 제공하는 것. 둘째, 픽업 유닛을 악기의 줄에 대하여 정확히 조정할 수 있는 장치를 제공하는 것. 셋째, 전체적으로 제조와 설치가 경제적이면서도 작동이 특히 신뢰할 만하고 효과적인, 소형의 조립체를 제공하는 것.”

누구나 눈치채는 그 디테일도 한 줄로 설명된다. “픽업 유닛은 줄에 직각으로 두기보다 예각으로 기울여 설치하는 것이 바람직한 것으로 밝혀졌다.”

media.note: US2573254 Fig.1~3 — 솔리드 바디, 3분할 새들, 몸통을 관통하는 줄 구멍이 모두 그려져 있음. 퍼블릭 도메인

blocks.b:
“문제는 딱 하나, ‘Broadcaster’라는 이름이었다. Gretsch가 이미 상표로 등록해 둔 상태였다.”

Fender의 해법은 회사 말로 이렇다. “항복하고 이 기발한 악기들을 매장과 카탈로그에서 빼는 대신, 우리는 재빨리 브랜딩을 손봤다. 헤드스톡에서 ‘Broadcaster’ 글자만 떼어내고, 새 모델을 계속 연주자들 손에 쥐여주었다.”

그 기타들을 지금은 Nocaster라고 부른다.

media.note: 헤드스톡 데칼 비교 3컷: Broadcaster → 이름이 잘려나간 'Nocaster' → Telecaster. 실물 사진 권리 확인 필요

blocks.b:
1951년, Leo Fender의 초기 동료 가운데 하나인 Don Randall이 Telecaster라는 이름을 제안했다. 텔레비전이 집집마다 들어가던 때였고, Fender는 거기에 올라타고 싶었다.

Fender는 이 개명이 “악기에 이렇다 할 변경을 가져오지도, 요구하지도 않았다”고 적는다.

겨냥한 시장은 웨스턴 스윙 연주자였다. 1940년대 말에서 1950년대 초까지 그 음악은 여전히 오락의 중심에 있었다.

Fender의 이야기에 따르면 Leo Fender와 George Fullerton은 이 기타를 들고 클럽을 돌며 웨스턴 스윙 연주자들에게 쥐여줬다. Jimmy Bryant에게 건넸을 때, 그는 쉬는 시간에 한 번 쳐보더니 남은 무대를 그 기타로 끝냈다. “많은 이들이 Bryant를 최초의 Telecaster 사용자로 꼽는다.”

Jimmy Wyble, Charlie Aldrich, Roy Watkins, Bill Carson이 뒤를 이었다. 다음은 홍키통크였다. Buck Owens, Luther Perkins, James Burton.

전시회에 나온 딜러들은 이 기타를 카누 노, 눈삽이라고 불렀다.

Fender는 1951년 4월 23일 바디 형태로 디자인 특허를 출원했다. 그해 8월에 등록됐다.

media.note: 1950~51년 펜더 광고 또는 NAMM 전시 사진 — 확보 필요. 없으면 디자인 특허 USD164227 도면(PD)으로 대체

blocks.b:
솔리드바디 전기 기타는 이미 있었다. 1941년 무렵의 Les Paul의 ‘로그’, 1948년 Paul Bigsby가 Merle Travis를 위해 만든 악기. 다만 모두 한 사람을 위해 손으로 만든 한 대짜리였다.

Telecaster는 볼트로 조립되는 부품에서 다량으로 찍어낼 수 있게 그려졌다. 지금도 사실상 같은 도면으로 만들어진다.

media.note: 1952 Les Paul Goldtop · 1954 Stratocaster 챕터 링크 카드. 생산 라인 사진이 있으면 좋음

blocks.b:
At the start of the 1940s Gibson had already been shown two solid-body electric guitars, the APP of the musician and inventor Orbra Wallace Appleton and Les Paul's Epiphone "Log". The company was not interested.

Fender showed the Esquire at the 1950 NAMM show, and almost every western swing guitarist took an interest. Paul Bigsby had built a solid body for Merle Travis, and Slingerland made a small one, the 401, but Fender was the first to produce them in quantity.

After the Esquire's success, Ted McCarty and Maurice Berlin decided that Gibson needed a solid body to compete with Fender. They gave the work to a team led by Larry Allers, under the sales director Clarence Havenga.

Fender cut its bodies from a flat board of ash. Gibson kept the carved top of its archtops. "Look, if we are going to make a guitar, we are going to make one that will be different than anything that Leo was making," McCarty said.

The first experiments, in 1950, resembled an ES-125: flat top and back, no cutaway, an unbound sunburst mahogany body and one P-90 in the centre. They were too large and heavy, and smaller flat-top guitars followed with RANGER written on the pickguard.

Next came a Florentine cutaway like the ES-140's, for the upper frets. Mahogany alone gave too little sustain, so Gibson tried maple, and maple with mahogany, with the grain running in different directions and the neck set at different angles.

One prototype from 1951 survives, kept by Larry Allers's son Ron: natural finish, a 25-inch scale and a carved top cut from one piece of maple, thick enough to show on both sides of the neck. It was later fitted with humbuckers and refinished in sunburst. Scott Lentz and David Flood returned it to its original finish in 1983.

With the guitar ready, Gibson needed a name and a way to sell it. McCarty always denied that the company had wanted to keep its own name off a solid body; signature models for Nick Lucas and Roy Smeck had already sold well. "So we made our solid-body guitar. Now we needed somebody with a reputation, a player to give it some publicity," he said.

From a list of candidates Gibson chose Les Paul, who had appeared in its 1939 and 1949 catalogues and had already been experimenting with solid bodies. He was playing Epiphones, and McCarty expected him to be hard to persuade.

Maurice Berlin sent his assistant, Mark Carlucci, to find the man with the "broomstick and the pickups on it". They met in Chicago. Les Paul assumed the new guitar had a flat top and grew enthusiastic when he heard it was carved.

McCarty brought the prototypes to Pennsylvania, where Les Paul was recording with Mary Ford. He played a few notes and said, "I think we should join them!"

The guitar would be called the Les Paul Model. Under a five-year contract he received 5 per cent of the profits, advised Gibson and played only Gibson guitars; until production began he was asked to put the Gibson logo on his Epiphones. The contract was renewed twice, for ten more years in all.

Les Paul asked for changes. The cutaway was to be rounded off: "It would knock your wrist if you weren't careful." The top was to be gold, which he thought would give the guitar a regal and unusual look. And it was to use a bridge he had developed in 1945 and already tried on one of his L-12s.

Gold had already been used on a custom ES-175 that Les Paul ordered as a present for a friend. "The finish in the guitar, the Goldtop, is bronze powder mixed in lacquer. That's what makes it reflective and brilliant," McCarty said.

The maple top was dense enough to need no sealer: a thin coat of nitrocellulose, the gold, and four coats of clear over it. Where the clear has worn away the bronze has oxidised and turned greenish. Collectors call these guitars Bullion Gold.

Les Paul filed the bridge on 9 July 1952 under his own name, Lester W. Polfuss, as a "combined bridge and tail piece for stringed instruments", assigned to Gibson. It was granted in 1956. A bar carried the strings and was held by two rods to a hinged plate at the bottom edge of the body. It could be set for height and length, though not string by string.

In the patent the strings are "passed over and rest upon the top of the bridge". Gibson's bar was nickel-plated brass, which wrapping would have worn through, and the low neck angle and short pickups pointed the same way, so the strings went under it. That ruled out the muting Les Paul liked, and strings picked hard slid sideways and went slightly out of tune.

Body and neck were Honduras mahogany, with the maple top glued on and carved more gently than on the prototypes. The neck, thick by later standards, carried Ted McHugh's truss rod. The Brazilian rosewood fingerboard had trapezoid inlays, a radius of 10 to 12 inches and, on the very first guitars, no binding. The scale was listed as 24.75 inches and measured 24.5625.

The pickups were two P-90s, the PU-90 model 480 single coil that Walt Fuller designed in the 1940s and Gibson introduced in 1946. Two volume controls, two tone controls and a three-way Switchcraft switch, at first without the plastic ring of later guitars.

Gibson announced the guitar in May 1952: "The guitar everyone has been waiting for and asking about is here at last! It's the new and smart-looking gold finished Gibson Les Paul Model, solid-body electric Spanish cutaway."

The first guitars reached dealers in June, listed at $210, plus $39.50 for the case. Gibson shipped 1,716 in 1952, 2,245 in 1953, 1,504 in 1954 and 862 in 1955.

Leo Fender developed the Precision Bass in 1950 and 1951, the first commercially successful solid-body electric bass guitar. Some music historians argue it had a bigger impact on popular music than either the Telecaster or the Stratocaster.

It also raised a question: what was it supposed to be plugged in to? Fender's own history answers, "There were no suitably powerful and reliable amps in 1951 made specifically for bass guitar, because there weren't any bass guitars."

When the Precision Bass reached music stores in November 1951, it was paired with Fender's TV-front Pro, a guitar amp whose single 15-inch speaker was at first thought adequate for the new instrument. It soon became clear that bassists needed an amp of their own.

Leo Fender and his staff were already building one, another TV-front 1×15, but it was not ready until 1952, when Fender's sales literature listed it simply as "Amplifier." Sales chief Don Randall soon named it the Bassman. Randall named all Fender amps of the era and all the instruments except the Precision Bass, which Leo named himself.

From the outside, the 1952 Bassman looked a lot like the Pro, in a cabinet of similar size. It had one channel, with two inputs and two knobs, volume and tone, on a panel at the top. A cable collectors call the "umbilical cord" ran from that panel down to a copper-plated steel chassis at the bottom, which held most of the electronics. It put about 26 watts into a Jensen P15N that Fender billed as "specially designed."

George Gruhn, quoted in Tom Wheeler's The Soul of Tone, says that with it Leo Fender "made the first amp that was worth calling a bass amp."

A schematic survives for what is believed to be an earlier Bassman, circuit 5A6, but no amp built to it has surfaced. Its circuit is that of the 1947 Dual Professional, which suggests someone relabeled that amp's drawing.

It was the first Fender amp with a closed back. The panel had two round ports, designed to bring out the bass; the Pro, like every other Fender guitar amp at the time, was open at the back.

Unlike the Bassmans that followed, this first one was really best suited to bass. It was made in very small numbers, and perhaps only 20 to 25 survive.

The 5B6 circuit went into the last of the TV-front cabinets and then into the new wide-panel cabinet, with a five-inch band of tweed above and below the grille cloth. Apart from its front it was essentially the same amp, and it kept its bottom chassis and its ported back.

Fender still sold it for bass alone. "It is not a hashed-over guitar amplifier," the catalog read, "but an instrument that has been designed for the reproduction of bass and bass only." A growing number of musicians were finding that it made a fine guitar and harmonica amp too.

A 15-inch speaker had been the obvious choice for deep, full bass, but its large cone tended to flub out when a low E was hit hard at volume, and Fender was hearing that the single speaker tended to blow.

The way forward was to divide the load among four smaller speakers, each of which had to move less and so was stressed less. In November 1954 Fender changed the Bassman radically: four 10-inch Jensen P10R speakers in a new narrow-panel cabinet. The first came as a small batch of prototypes that November and December, and according to Dave Hunter of Vintage Guitar only 11 of those early 5D6s survive.

The 5D6 was designed by Freddie Tavares, a longtime member of Fender's research and development staff. Bill Carson credited the four-speaker Bassman to him: "Leo was working on something else at the time. Freddie put this thing together." The aim was a bass amp that guitar players could use too. Leo Fender did not play guitar; Tavares did.

It had two rectifier tubes, and became known as the dual-rectifier Bassman, a name Mesa/Boogie would later take up. With a new output transformer and a fixed-bias output stage, its power rose from about 26 watts to 40. It still had only two inputs, labeled normal and bright, a sign that Fender knew guitarists were using it.

At low volume it gave sparkling clean tones, particularly with the new guitar of 1954, the Stratocaster. Tom Wheeler: "At louder volumes it thickens with a sweet distortion that only seems to get creamier the more it's cranked."

Otis Rush told Guitar Player how he found the combination: "I watched Earl Hooker. He had a Strat, so I bought one. He had an old Fender Bassman, so I got that. Put them together and developed a hell of a sound."

The narrow-panel cabinet, with a strip of tweed just over an inch wide above and below the grille, stayed until the end of the tweed era in 1960. Inside, small revisions followed through the 5D6-A, 5E6 and 5E6-A.

Demand grew quickly: by the middle of 1957 Fender had sold more than 1,500 5E6s. Its 1955 catalog called the Bassman "an excellent amplifier for bass but it is also an excellent amplifier for other musical instruments." George Fullerton, Leo Fender's partner, said he considered the tweed Bassman the best amplifier Fender ever built.

In July 1957 Fender changed the design again. The 5F6 replaced the two rectifiers with a single 83 mercury-vapor tube, added a three-knob tone stack with separate treble, middle and bass, and swapped the cathodyne phase inverter for a long-tailed pair, for more clean power and headroom.

It also had four inputs, high and low gain on each of two channels; at the time one large amp often served a whole band, bass, guitar, harmonica and even vocals. Wheeler wrote that it seemed to "combine the perfect array of preamp components, output tubes, power, negative feedback loop, passive tone controls, cab, baffle, and speakers."

In 1958 came the final change, model 5F6-A: a GZ34 rectifier in place of the mercury-vapor tube, with matching changes to the presence control and the feedback loop. It is this version that made the Bassman's reputation as perhaps the greatest amp of all time, and the 1959 amps so often singled out use exactly the same circuit as the 1958s.

Andy Marshall of THD, one of the first to build a high-quality copy, points to its large-core, interleaved Triad output transformer as critical. In 1960 Fender moved to Jensen P10Q speakers, which handled more power and gave better clean tones than the P10Rs.

Famously, it was the 5F6-A that Jim Marshall and his colleagues copied, part for part, to make their JTM45. A ban on importing musical instruments from the US to the UK had stayed in place until 1959, and in 1961 American amps were still hard to get.

A US serviceman going home had sold a tweed Bassman to Marshall's shop. It went to the bass player of Adam Faith's band, the Roulettes; when the band took a Vox endorsement, it came back for £60, and Marshall's technician Ken Bran drew a schematic from it. By late 1962 they had a prototype, and at first they built one amp from Monday to Friday and sold it on Saturday to buy the parts for the next. The copy was so close that its switches worked upside down: down for on.

Everyone in Buck Owens and the Buckaroos used Bassmans. T-Bone Walker, B.B. King and Buddy Holly played 4×10s, Rory Gallagher used a 1954 Bassman alone or alongside his Vox AC30, Robbie Robertson used tweed Bassmans in The Last Waltz, and Heart's Howard Leese recorded "Barracuda" with one.

Buddy Guy, who used them on many of his Chess recordings, told Guitar Player about a night when he had "this little Fender Bassman amplifier which was blowing the big ones off the stage." The next night, he said, the other group asked never to be sent on after him.

In 1961 Fender changed the Bassman radically once more, into a separate head and speaker cabinet covered in blonde Tolex, and the tweed era was over.

In 1990 Fender began reissuing a Bassman based on the 5F6-A, built in Corona, California, with four Eminence alnico speakers and a solid-state rectifier. Production later moved to Ensenada, Baja California, and the '59 Bassman LTD went back to a GZ34 and Jensen P10Rs. In 1990 Stevie Ray Vaughan replaced the Super Reverbs in his touring rig with a pair of the newly released reissues.

Billy Gibbons: "When all is said and done, I go back to the house and I plug into a 4×10 Bassman and just turn it up."

blocks.b:
By 1953 Fender was seven years old. It had put the Telecaster and the Precision Bass on the market, along with steel guitars and amplifiers, and it was run by Leo Fender, a self-taught electronics man who did not play guitar.

Gibson had answered the Telecaster with the Les Paul in 1952. Don Randall, Fender's sales chief, once called the Telecaster "plain Jane."

Leo Fender listened to working players, Rex Gallion and Bill Carson above all. Gallion, a country and western guitarist, is quoted as asking him, "Why not get away from a body that is always digging into your ribs?" Carson wanted a body that fitted like a shirt.

The answer was what Leo called contours: a scoop cut into the back and a bevel on the front where the picking arm rests. George Fullerton gave Gallion and Carson about equal credit for them, and said his wife came up with the name "Original Contour."

Leo said the guitar was begun because of the vibrato: "All the salesmen were asking for a vibrato, and so the [Stratocaster] was begun." For Randall, "The Stratocaster's introduction was market driven."

The accounts of when work started do not agree. Leo said the neck, body and pickups were designed before Fender moved to its new factory on Valencia Drive in June 1953. Fullerton dated the first pickup work to the end of 1951; Carson remembered Leo first talking about the guitar in 1952.

Freddie Tavares, a steel guitarist from Hawaii who played the slide that opens the Looney Tunes theme, began working part-time for Leo in March 1953. No drawings of the new guitar existed yet. "We had a piece of paper with lines drawn on it: six lines for the strings, and two cross lines for the nut and the bridge," Tavares said. They drew a body over the lines, erasing until they liked the shape.

The model was the Precision Bass, Leo's first two-horned body. In early 1953 Don Randall named the guitar: after the Broadcaster and the Telecaster, the Stratocaster.

Like the Telecaster, the Stratocaster had a one-piece maple neck bolted to the body with four screws. The new headstock put the six tuners in a row so the strings ran straight from the nut. It resembles the headstock Paul Bigsby made for Merle Travis; Leo never credited Bigsby and said the idea came from a photograph of a Croatian musician.

Kluson tuners were not made to sit in a line, so their strips had to be cut to fit.

Leo blamed the Telecaster's worst faults on its pickups: uneven output from string to string, and feedback. The new single coils had staggered pole pieces to balance the heavy strings of the day, the B pole shortest and the D pole tallest.

There were three of them. Leo said Fender had plenty of three-position switches in stock; Tavares remembered him saying, "Let's put three pickups. Two is good, but three will kill 'em!" The bridge pickup was slanted, and pickups and controls sat on the pickguard, which dropped into the body as one unit.

The switch was meant to give one pickup at a time. Players found they could balance it between positions and get two.

The vibrato took longest. The first design gave each string a roller and anchored the strings in a separate tailpiece, and Leo tooled up the factory before testing it. Fender's inventory for December 1953 listed 400 Stratocaster bridges, 5,240 bridge rollers and 1,080 tremolo lever sockets.

The rollers let the strings move sideways and soaked up their energy. Carson said the guitar "sounded like an amplified banjo with no sustain." Randall had wanted to show it at the summer 1953 NAMM show in Chicago, and it was not ready.

The design that worked moved the whole bridge with the strings. Fender says Leo took the idea from a gram scale. The strings passed up through a steel inertia block under the bridge plate and over six saddles, each set for height and length. Six screws at the front of the plate formed a pivot, and springs in a cavity at the back, three at first and then five, held the bridge floating against the pull of the strings.

Leo filed for a patent on 30 August 1954. Its first stated object was a tremolo for guitars "played in such manner that one hand is in the region of the bridge, there being a tremolo control arm so arranged as to fit within the palm of the players hand." It was granted on 10 April 1956 as US 2,741,146, and does not mention the contoured body.

Fender announced the Stratocaster in the April 1954 issue of International Musician. A letter to dealers said shipments were expected to begin on 15 May, and a small pre-production run had already started; the first full production run followed in October. Its advertising called it the "Comfort Contoured" Stratocaster.

It cost $249.50 with the vibrato and $229.50 without. It was Fender's first sunburst, dark Salem shading to canary yellow over ash, added at Randall's insistence.

The Stratocaster got off to a slow start. Three years after its introduction it was still "not particularly well known," Tom Wheeler writes. Fender put it in the hands of the western swing and pop players Leo had in mind, among them Buddy Merrill of Lawrence Welk's band and Alvino Rey.

On 1 December 1957 the Crickets played "That'll Be the Day" and "Peggy Sue" on The Ed Sullivan Show. Their singer and guitarist was Buddy Holly, 21, playing a Stratocaster.

Fender kept changing it. Alder replaced ash in mid-1956, and alnico 5 magnets replaced alnico 3 late that year. A red band joined the sunburst in 1958. In 1959 a rosewood fingerboard was glued onto the maple neck, and the walnut "skunk stripe" down the back was no longer needed.

Gretsch was founded in Brooklyn in 1883 by Friedrich Gretsch, a 27-year-old German immigrant who made tambourines and drums. His grandson Fred Gretsch Jr. took over in 1942 and, after serving in the Navy during the Second World War, ran the company until it was sold in 1967.

Those years took in what became Gretsch's golden era, from 1953 to 1965.

Jimmie Webster, born in Ohio in 1908, had tuned pianos and run a small music store in New York before he began consulting for Gretsch. By the 1950s he was the company's idea man, and 1954 was his year.

He led Gretsch to offer custom colors, the first company to do so: Cadillac Green, Jaguar Tan and Copper Mist. He covered the tops of Duo Jets with laminates from the drum division to make the Silver Jet. And at that summer's NAMM show he unveiled his dream guitar, the White Falcon, built as a concept; dealers wanted it so badly that Gretsch added it to the 1955 line.

Gretsch was floundering in the wake of Gibson's success with Les Paul as an endorser, and Webster set his sights on Chet Atkins for the company's first signature model.

At first Atkins resisted. He was happy playing his own modified D'Angelico. He gave in to Webster's promise that he could design his own model.

The first prototype, sent to Atkins in mid-1954, was a special-order Streamliner with a second DeArmond DynaSonic pickup, a lightly figured maple top, 21 frets and gold hardware.

Gretsch was a Brooklyn company, with its own ideas about what a guitar for a Nashville artist should look like. The finish was an amber red fading to transparent orange. A large G was branded into the top and a steer's head inlaid on the headstock; the tailpiece looked like a belt buckle, and cactus and steer heads were etched into the fingerboard markers.

Atkins did not care for the country trimmings, and as he and the guitar grew more popular he had them removed one by one.

Atkins asked for a Bigsby vibrato and a brass nut for better sustain. The second prototype, the one thought of as the first 6120, had a fixed-arm Bigsby B6 with an aluminum Bigsby bridge, a fancier maple top, the brass nut and a gold Lucite pickguard.

There is footage of Atkins playing his 1954 hit "Mr. Sandman" on that guitar.

By the time the production guitar was ready, Atkins had asked for a 22-fret neck. The body was 15½ inches wide, though the catalog said 16, and 2¾ inches deep. Gretsch built guitars in batches of 50 or 100; it began making the model in late 1954 and selling it early in 1955, at $385.

The 6120 drew on everything Gretsch had learned about hollow-body guitars, and it sold well from the start. As Edward Ball put it in his history of the model, "the legend had begun."

Gretsch kept changing the guitar, sometimes in the middle of a batch and more often than it reprinted its catalogs, which still frustrates collectors trying to date one. Only three batches of 6120s were made in 1955: the Brooklyn factory could build about 2,000 guitars a year, and eight other models were in production.

Eddie Cochran's 1955 came from the second batch, and "Summertime Blues" made him an international star in 1958. Duane Eddy bought his 6120 new on 20 September 1957. Playing melodies on the bass strings through its DeArmond pickups and Bigsby, he made the twang that would long be associated with Gretsch.

In 1956 the gold Bigsby gave way to plain aluminum, the fixed arm to a swivel, and the etched markers to plain blocks. Atkins had never liked the big f-holes and asked for a solid top; Gretsch, in a moment of simple genius, painted smaller f-holes on.

In 1957 the western styling began to go. The G was removed from the top, G-shaped knobs arrived, the orange was toned down toward brown, and hump-block markers made their debut.

1958 brought the biggest changes. Thumbnail markers replaced the hump blocks, and trestle bracing across the top and back improved sustain and reduced feedback.

Atkins had never liked the DynaSonic pickups, which he found bass-heavy, short of top end and noisy. Ray Butts, who had designed the EchoSonic amp, wired two coils out of phase to cancel the hum, and the Filter'Tron won Atkins over at once. Made in-house, it spread across the whole line, and a three-way tone switch replaced the tone knob.

In 1959 a zero fret arrived, for the lower action Atkins wanted. In 1960 the Bigsby gained a V cutout and the body was cut to 2½ inches deep.

In 1970 Joe Walsh gave Pete Townshend a 1960 6120. "I opened the case and it was bright orange and I thought, ugh, it's horrible," Townshend remembered. Then he plugged it in. Through a 1959 Fender Bandmaster it became the sound of "Won't Get Fooled Again" and "Bargain" on Who's Next.

In 1961 the body shrank to 2¼ inches, and in 1962 came the biggest change yet: a double-cutaway body with sealed f-holes, two inches deep. Atkins himself had pushed for it.

George Harrison never had an endorsement deal with Gretsch, but he did more than anyone for demand. Production rose from 2,000 guitars a year to 12,000, and Gretsch still could not keep up.

In 1967 Fred Gretsch Jr. sold the company to Baldwin for about $4 million and 10,000 shares. In 1970 Baldwin moved production from Brooklyn to Booneville, Arkansas, and almost none of the original workforce went with it. By 1972 the 6120 had become the 7660, without its orange finish.

In 1979 Fred Gretsch Jr. died, and Atkins decided to end his long relationship with the company.

In 1985 Fred W. Gretsch, Friedrich's great-grandson, bought the company back. Atkins was now with Gibson, so the 6120 returned as the Nashville, built in Japan.

Its obvious champion was Brian Setzer, who had bought his first 6120 in the late 1970s on Long Island and played a 1960 model through the Stray Cats' rise. Signature 6120s followed for Setzer, for Duane Eddy and for Eddie Cochran.

The story goes that Leo Fender received a shipment of hardwood too narrow for his lap steel guitars, and rather than let it go unused, designed amplifiers around it. These were the "woodies"; the metal strips on the front were supposedly Leo's attempt at a stylish, automotive look.

The earliest Deluxes carried the designation Model 26 on the control panel. They had a 10-inch speaker and octal tubes, three inputs, two for instruments and one for a microphone, two volume controls and one tone control.

TV-front Deluxes, covered in tweed, were made from 1948 to 1954. Their phase inverter was less hi-fi than the ones that came later and gave the sound a certain grittiness: there isn't much headroom, but the overdrive is a wonderful thing.

The wide-panel Deluxe of 1954 and 1955 was a transitional model. It was the first to use the miniature nine-pin preamp tubes common today, a 12AY7 and a 12AX7, like the narrow-panel amps to come.

Then came the narrow-panel 5E3, produced from 1955 to 1960 and the pinnacle of tweed Deluxe circuits.

In broad strokes it makes between 10 and 14 watts from a pair of 6V6 power tubes and a 5Y3 rectifier, into a single 12-inch speaker. The cabinet is about the size of a modern Princeton.

The 5E3 had a different phase inverter and more voltage, which gave it more clean headroom and its unique midrange snarl.

Carl Carrasco of Carl's Custom Amps: "It's absolutely a classic-sounding amp. There's not a lot of cleans there, but they are angelic, and the overdrive is gritty, warm and punchy."

Fender used many different transformers in these years, and that, along with variation in the other components, is one reason tweed Deluxes differ so much from amp to amp.

Neil Young has famously searched a lifetime for a backup to his favorite 1959 Deluxe. He has come close, he says, but never quite found its equal.

A narrow-panel Deluxe is said to have been one of the early house amps at Rudy Van Gelder's studio, where so many Blue Note jazz guitar parts were recorded; the very early Grant Green records give a taste of it.

Larry Carlton's famous 5E3 can be heard at the start of Steely Dan's "Don't Take Me Alive."

Scotty Moore, Steve Cropper, Don Felder, the Edge and Neil Young were or are famous 5E3 users, and Mike Campbell pairs one with a non-reverb blackface Princeton on stage.

Vintage 5E3s are expensive, but there are lots of clones to choose from.

From 1961 to 1963 Fender built the brownface Deluxe, in brown Tolex with a wheat grille. It added tremolo and two channels, normal and bright, and moved from cathode bias to fixed bias.

Cathode-bias amps like the tweeds have more sag and a spongier feel, and distort sooner; fixed-bias amps are firmer and stay cleaner longer. The brownface made a dependable 15 watts, and Ted Nugent's "Cat Scratch Fever" was recorded with one.

In 1963 the blackface Deluxe arrived, and with it the Deluxe Reverb.

The tweed has never gone away. Two Deluxes in Fender's current catalog, the '57 Custom Deluxe and the Edge's signature Deluxe, are based on the narrow-panel 5E3 circuit.

By 1957, sales of Gibson's new solid-body guitars had begun to slip, while thinline models like the Byrdland had picked up slightly. Gibson concluded that players might be drawn to less feedback but still wanted traditional-looking guitars.

Its sales force was also grumbling that Gibson's reputation for innovation was lagging behind the upstarts at Fender, and in the America of the 1950s, seeming modern carried a lot of weight.

Gibson answered with the Explorer and the Flying V, which may have overshot the market by about 25 years. For players who wanted a traditional shape, it made a new double-cutaway guitar.

Ted McCarty, Gibson's president, described the idea: a block of wood in the middle, like a solid-body guitar, with hollow wings. "The block made it stiffer, so it had a brighter tone than that acoustic wood. It looked like an acoustic, but it wasn't acoustic. It was an electric."

Gibson revealed the guitar to dealers in the Gibson Gazette in February 1958, under the headline "new ES-335T Spanish guitar." It appeared in the March catalog, and the very first one came off the production line on 21 April 1958.

The sunburst listed for $267.50 and the natural finish for $282.50; a brown case cost another $46.50. That year a Les Paul Junior listed for $120, and a Super 400 for $700.

The 335 was 16 inches wide at the lower bout, with a laminated top, back and sides: three plies, two of maple around softer poplar. Inside ran a solid maple center block about four inches wide, the same thickness as the rims.

The one-piece mahogany neck was glued into that block like a Les Paul's and joined the body at the 19th fret, against the 14th on an ES-175, which left the upper frets of its 22-fret rosewood board within easy reach.

It had two humbuckers with Gibson's new PAF stickers under nickel covers, and the patented Tune-o-matic ABR-1 bridge. Two volume and two tone knobs sat on the top, and the output jack was on the face of the guitar.

Dot markers were inlaid in the fingerboard and a crown on the headstock, and an orange label could be seen inside the treble-side f-hole.

The guitar was officially launched at the summer 1958 NAMM show in Chicago. Late in the model year Gibson bound the fingerboard and changed the three-ply laminate to four ply, likely because early tops tended to crack near the output jack. The slightly pointed early cutaways had become rounded by the fall: the "Mickey Mouse ears" collectors prize.

In 1959 the frets got slightly bigger and the neck slightly fuller, changes that together make it the most desirable year.

By the end of 1958 Gibson had moved forward with the flagship ES-355, in cherry red with an ebony fingerboard, block inlays, a Bigsby and gold-plated hardware. The ES-345 followed early in 1959, with stereo wiring and a Varitone tone switch.

In 1959 the price list ran from $279.50 for the 335 to $550 for the 355.

By 1960 Gibson had a success on its hands: the 335 had sold about 500. Gibson had hoped jazz players would embrace it; instead it was blues and rock players who took up the semi-solid guitars.

B.B. King settled on a 335 with a Bigsby, stereo wiring and a Varitone, the guitar he played on Live at the Regal in November 1964. "It was like somebody knew what kind of guitar I'd been wanting," he said. Freddie King moved to a 345 and later a 355, and around 1960 Chuck Berry took up a 335.

In 1962 Gibson changed the 335's fingerboard markers from dots to small blocks. That year Ritchie Blackmore bought a cherry 335 with a Bigsby at Jim Marshall's shop in London, and used it on the first two Deep Purple records.

Alvin Lee bought a dot-neck 335 for £45 in his hometown of Nottingham. Covered in stickers, including its famous peace sign, it went with him to Woodstock.

Eric Clapton bought a cherry 1964 335 in November 1968, a couple of weeks before Cream's last two shows at the Royal Albert Hall, and played it all evening. He went on using it in Blind Faith and on later blues records.

Forty years later, with its original case, it sold at auction for $850,000 to benefit his Crossroads rehabilitation centre.

Larry Carlton wanted something more versatile than his Les Paul, Telecaster and ES-175 for session work. "I wanted a guitar that felt kind of like a jazz box but didn't have to sound like a jazz box," he said, "and the 335 seemed to me to be obviously the choice."

He chose his from three on the wall of a shop in 1969. It became part of the West Coast sound with the Crusaders and on Steely Dan's The Royal Scam, and he still plays it on the road.

In 1981 Gibson went back to the original drawings and vintage examples to build a reissue: a one-piece mahogany neck, the old rim shape and top arch, rounder horns, PAF-style pickups and the ABR-1 bridge. It came out as the ES-335 Dot.

It listed for $995, at a time when an original 1959 dot-neck could still be bought for around $2,500.

blocks.b:
Les Paul sales peaked in 1956 and 1957, with the Junior by far the biggest seller: 3,129 in 1956 alone. Solid-body guitars were still a minority in the marketplace, though, and sales of the Goldtop had begun to slip.

In 1958, to excite the market, Gibson switched the Standard to a new cherry sunburst finish. The look lasted only until 1960, but the guitars of those years, the 'Bursts, are seen today as the apex of Les Paul construction, and 1959 as the year Gibson got it all right.

In Gibson's electronics lab, Seth Lover had been charged with cutting down the hum of the P-90. He thought of the choke coil in amplifiers, which helps eliminate the hum of the power transformer. "I thought, if we can make humbucking chokes, why can't we make humbucking pickups?"

His pickup wired two coils of opposite magnetic polarity out of phase, so that the hum cancelled. It did more than cancel the hum: it gave a completely new, fatter sound. The salesmen asked for adjustable screws, something more to talk about to dealers, and early in 1957 the new pickups replaced the P-90s on the Goldtop and the Custom.

Lover applied for a patent in June 1955. His was not the first humbucking design, and proving what made it different took until 28 July 1959. Meanwhile a small sticker on the base of each pickup read "Patent Applied For", and the name PAF stuck.

Gibson kept putting the stickers on into 1960, it is believed so that competitors would have a harder time finding the patent and the information in it. When a patent number finally appeared on the pickups in 1962, it was the number of a bridge patent Gibson already held.

The first Standards in the new finish shipped on 28 May 1958, in time for that summer's NAMM show in Chicago, listed at $247.50. Under the opaque gold the maple had been hidden. Now it could be seen, and the builders had to bookmatch the top: a piece sliced through the centre and opened like a book, so the grain is symmetrical on both sides.

Les Pauls had not been selling well and were not a priority for the fancier pieces of maple, so many bursts have fairly plain tops. If one has a flamed top, it was more by chance than by design.

The body was a one-piece Honduran mahogany back under a two-piece Eastern maple top, a harder wood than Western maple. The maple was often quarter-sawn, which can produce the flame these guitars are known for, and the two were glued with hot hide glue, which dries to a hard crystal and helps carry vibration.

The carve of a fifties top is deep and pronounced, almost a waist where it catches the light. No Les Paul after that decade has duplicated it properly.

The Tune-o-matic bridge and stop tailpiece, which arrived in 1955, made the guitar more stable and let it intonate better than ever. On a 1959 the bridge was a nickel-plated ABR-1 with brass saddles and the tailpiece was aluminium, on studs anchored an inch deep in the body, against seven-eighths of an inch today.

That depth, length and choice of materials, Sam Ash says, made guitars that rang like a bell, with the sustain the Les Paul is known for.

For 1959 Gibson made a few more tweaks. The frets grew from about .090 to .100 of an inch, and the big, bat-like neck of 1958 became a slimmer rounded C. One that Sam Ash measured was about .872 of an inch deep at the first fret: big enough to be comfortable, small enough to play fast. Each was carved by hand, and each varied.

The Brazilian rosewood fingerboard had a 12-inch radius and cellulose trapezoid inlays. A holly veneer faced the headstock, angled back at 17 degrees, and the Kluson single-ring tuners have shrunk and yellowed over the years.

No two PAFs were quite alike. They were wound with 42-gauge enamel wire of a purplish hue around a long Alnico magnet, chosen at random from grades 2, 3, 4 or 5. The Leesona 102 winders had no automatic stop that could be relied on, so workers timed the wind, and readings ran from about 7k to 9k.

When players took the covers off to brighten the treble, they found bobbins of different colours. Eastman Chemical had run out of the black plastic, so Gibson used white for a while, sometimes one of each. Seth Lover found the debate funny: whatever made pickups differ, it was not bobbin colour.

Gibson filled the backs with cherry red pore filler and sprayed the tops with aniline dye, which fades in sunlight. Shop windows, smoky clubs, years at home between sessions: each guitar faded differently, the red lightening or darkening into what collectors call lemon burst, iced tea burst or dark burst. In 1960 Gibson changed to a more vibrant sunburst that did not fade so much.

The nitrocellulose lacquer had no plasticiser, so as it heated and cooled it checked into fine cracks, a look some players now pay extra for.

None of it did much for sales. The Standard sold 434 in 1958 and 643 in 1959, then fell back in 1960. Gibson had just added a third expansion to its Kalamazoo factory and needed sales to pay for it, so in 1961 it replaced the single-cutaway carved top with a flat, double-cutaway design, now called the SG.

By Joe Bonamassa's count, about 1,700 sunbursts shipped between 1958 and 1960. "So they're not incredibly rare," he says, "just incredibly sought-after."

By 1965 British blues players were looking for the instruments their American heroes played. Eric Clapton had seen Freddie King pictured with a Goldtop on an album cover, and in May 1965, while he was with John Mayall's Bluesbreakers, he found a used sunburst in almost new condition in a London shop.

The Bluesbreakers album, nicknamed "Beano" for the comic Clapton reads on its cover, came out in July 1966 and launched the Les Paul into a cranked Marshall sound. The guitar was stolen around the time Cream began rehearsing and has never been found. "I never really found one as good as that again," he said.

Clapton sent players scrambling for the old Standards. Keith Richards bought one on tour with the Rolling Stones in the States. Peter Green, who took Clapton's place in the Bluesbreakers, went on to use his on the early Fleetwood Mac records, and Jeff Beck bought a '59 in 1966 and played it on the Yardbirds' Roger the Engineer.

Mike Bloomfield found one in May 1967 and played it at the Monterey Pop Festival: "All of us were playing the same model guitar." In the summer of 1968 Billy Gibbons found the burst later named Pearly Gates.

Prices for old Les Pauls began to climb, and Gibson was moved by the demand too. It brought the Goldtop and the Custom to the 1968 NAMM show with the words "Okay, you win. We are pleased to announce that more of the original Les Paul Gibsons are available."

Today Mike Long of ATB Guitars puts a 1959 with its original parts and case at £300,000 to £600,000, and celebrity guitars such as Peter Green's Greeny, Jimmy Page's Number One and Billy Gibbons's Pearly Gates fetch a great deal more. "They are considered desirable because of their legacy more than anything else," he says.
